author: David Parnas
title: On the Criteria To Be Used in Decomposing Systems into Modules
claim: Modules should hide decisions likely to change, rather than simply mirror successive processing steps.
limit: An architectural argument illustrated by a small software example; it does not evaluate LLM teams.
use: Separate agent boundaries around information and authority, not a theatrical list of job titles.

author: Lisanne Bainbridge
title: Ironies of Automation
claim: Automating routine work can leave people responsible for rare, difficult exceptions while reducing their opportunity to practise.
limit: Industrial control analysis predates language models; the application here is an analogy.
use: Review capability and human attention are part of the system being commissioned.

author: Eric Horvitz
title: Principles of Mixed-Initiative User Interfaces
claim: Initiative should account for uncertain goals, the cost of interruption and opportunities for useful collaboration.
limit: Design principles and systems examples, not a universal rule for when an agent should ask permission.
use: Design escalation around the decision and its reversibility.

author: Michael Wooldridge and Nicholas Jennings
title: Intelligent Agents: Theory and Practice
claim: Surveys agency through autonomy, social ability, reactivity and proactiveness, alongside stronger conceptions of agents.
limit: A conceptual survey predating language models; these properties do not establish a system’s usefulness or safety.
use: Describe the environment, perceptions, goals and actions before choosing a contemporary agent framework.

author: Richard Sutton
title: The Bitter Lesson
claim: General methods that exploit computation have repeatedly displaced hand-built domain knowledge in AI.
limit: A historical argument about research progress, not evidence that any particular automated loop is worth continuing.
use: Scalable search still needs a useful objective and a way to recognize improvement.

author: D. Sculley and colleagues
title: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems
claim: Dependencies, entanglement and feedback loops can make a small model component expensive to maintain.
limit: A systems analysis of ML production risks rather than an agent benchmark.
use: Follow contracts from source data through evaluation to the person using the result.

author: Shunyu Yao and colleagues
title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
claim: Interleaving reasoning and actions lets observations inform subsequent steps in the evaluated tasks.
limit: Published benchmark results depend on models, tasks, tools and prompts; not a claim of general autonomous competence.
use: Treat the action-observation loop as a design object.

author: John Yang, Carlos Jimenez and colleagues
title: SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
claim: The interface through which an agent navigates and edits a repository affects its ability to solve issues.
limit: Repository issue benchmarks do not evaluate animation quality or enjoyment.
use: Usable tools are a substantive part of agent design.

author: Noah Shinn and colleagues
title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
claim: Textual feedback retained across attempts can improve performance under the paper's task and feedback conditions.
limit: Episodic language feedback, not weight training; benefits depend on the quality of the feedback.
use: Memory should change the next attempt for a defensible reason.

author: Jie Huang and colleagues
title: Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
claim: In the tested settings, requests for intrinsic self-correction without external feedback often failed and could worsen answers.
limit: The title is dated: it is not a timeless impossibility result for all models or all feedback.
use: Separate fresh evidence from another confident reading of the same mistake.

author: Mert Cemri, Melissa Pan, Shuyi Yang and colleagues
title: Why Do Multi-Agent LLM Systems Fail?
claim: MAST organizes recurring failures in specification, coordination and verification across multi-agent traces.
limit: The study combines manual analysis and scaled labeling; a taxonomy can suggest questions without proving the cause of this studio's failures.
use: Use failure categories to inspect traces, not to assign blame by role name.

author: Yubin Kim and colleagues
title: Towards a Science of Scaling Agent Systems
claim: Benefits of multiple agents depend on task structure, architecture and coordination overhead in controlled comparisons.
limit: 180 configurations across four benchmarks; fitted relationships are not universal thresholds.
use: Choose parallelism after identifying independent work and shared bottlenecks.

author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Elizabeth Barnes and David Rein
title: Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity
claim: Sixteen experienced developers completing 246 tasks took 19% longer with the evaluated AI tools despite expecting a speedup.
limit: Mature repositories, familiar developers and early-2025 tools; neither all developers nor all future tools.
use: Measure useful completion rather than trusting perceived speed.

author: Joel Becker, Nate Rush, Tom Cunningham, David Rein and Khalid Mahamud
title: We are Changing our Developer Productivity Experiment Design
claim: The follow-up discusses selection effects and measurement problems that prevent a reliable simple speedup estimate.
limit: The later study does not establish a clean reversal of the earlier result.
use: Date productivity claims and retain uncertainty about changing tools and samples.

author: Alexander Novikov and colleagues
title: AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
claim: Generated programs are searched, executed and selected using automated evaluation and a population of candidates.
limit: Demonstrated in domains with tractable evaluators; subjective game quality is a different measurement problem.
use: Spend generation on candidates whose quality can be tested, while preserving diversity.

author: Joon Sung Park and colleagues
title: Generative Agents: Interactive Simulacra of Human Behavior
claim: Memory, retrieval, reflection and planning support believable behavior in a 25-agent town demonstration.
limit: Believability studies and short simulations do not prove enjoyable gameplay, social validity or reliable long-term planning.
use: Separate an interesting character architecture from the requirements of a playable game.

author: Erik Schluntz and Barry Zhang
title: Building effective agents
claim: Distinguishes predefined workflows from agents choosing their own next actions and recommends the simplest sufficient arrangement.
limit: Vendor engineering experience, not a randomized comparison of all architectures.
use: Give autonomy only where adaptive choice is useful.

author: Anthropic Engineering
title: How we built our multi-agent research system
claim: Parallel research agents helped cover independent information needs, with substantial token overhead.
limit: Reported internal gains and token comparisons are context-specific and not equal-budget proof for software development.
use: Separate breadth-first research from tightly coupled edits to one implementation.

author: Justin Young
title: Effective harnesses for long-running agents
claim: An initializer, incremental work, durable progress records and end-to-end checks help bridge limited context windows.
limit: Product engineering lessons; neither a guarantee of long-run quality nor an argument for endless continuation.
use: Design a recoverable unit of work and an observable stopping condition.

author: Anthropic Engineering
title: Demystifying evals for AI agents
claim: Agent evaluation must distinguish what the transcript says from the resulting world state and use suitable graders.
limit: Grader validity still needs calibration; model judgments are not independent ground truth.
use: Give each release claim an evaluator capable of observing it.

author: Ryan Lopopolo
title: Harness engineering
claim: Describes making an application's UI, diagnostics and repository conventions legible to coding agents.
limit: Vendor case study; reported code volume and speed estimates are not a causal productivity experiment.
use: Make the real application available for inspection instead of expanding instructions indefinitely.

author: Nicholas Carlini
title: Building a C compiler with a team of parallel Claudes
claim: A compiler harness exposed independent bugs for parallel workers; executable checks sustained substantial generation.
limit: Capability experiment with substantial cost and remaining compatibility limits; no matched single-agent economic comparison.
use: A verifier can make coupled work separable without establishing equal-cost efficiency.

author: Diane Sarkis
title: Building agents: When to fold subagents into your main agent loop
claim: Some router, planner and domain-agent layers can be replaced by a main loop with progressively supplied context.
limit: Enterprise implementation experience, not a universal verdict against subagents.
use: Retain separate agents where parallelism, verification or permission boundaries justify them.

author: Boris Tane
title: How I use Claude Code
claim: Describes research and repeated owner annotations on a written plan before implementation.
limit: One experienced practitioner's method, with no controlled productivity comparison.
use: Use a plan as a place where consequential disagreement becomes concrete.

author: Peter Steinberger
title: Shipping at Inference-Speed
claim: Emphasizes fast, executable feedback and architectural judgment while using coding agents intensively.
limit: Self-report with dated tool preferences; fast output does not by itself establish quality or transferability.
use: Contrast rapid iteration with deliberate plan annotation rather than pretending one style fits every task.

author: Mitchell Hashimoto
title: My AI adoption journey
claim: Describes learning agent limits through repeated work, selecting suitable tasks and improving the harness.
limit: Personal account, not evidence that unattended work is always efficient.
use: Commission work whose success can be checked when the agent returns.

author: Simon Willison
title: Agentic Engineering Patterns
claim: Collects emerging practices for working with coding agents, including verification and managing inexpensive code generation.
limit: A living, evolving guide; individual recommendations have different evidence bases.
use: Distinguish the cost of producing code from the responsibility for understanding and maintaining it.

author: Armin Ronacher
title: A year of vibes
claim: Reflects on changes to programming practice, failure history and the human responsibility that remains.
limit: Personal retrospective; preferences and forecasts are not measured laws.
use: Keep the history that explains a decision, including failed attempts.

author: Yichao Ji
title: Context Engineering for AI Agents: Lessons from Building Manus
claim: Explains stable prefixes, cache-aware context, file-backed memory and preserving errors in an agent loop.
limit: Provider and product experience; historical prices must not be reused as current cost estimates.
use: Memory design affects both what the agent sees and how much repeated context it processes.

author: Dex Horthy
title: 12-Factor Agents
claim: Places focused agent behavior inside software with explicit control flow, state and recoverable execution.
limit: A design manifesto and implementation guidance rather than a benchmark.
use: Keep durable application obligations outside an unbounded conversation.

author: Geoffrey Huntley
title: Ralph Wiggum as a software engineer
claim: Describes repeated agent invocation around a persistent task/specification and feedback.
limit: The living page includes anecdotes and broad claims; a loop is a mechanism, not proof of return on investment.
use: Ask what changes between iterations and what makes the loop stop.

author: Steve Yegge
title: Welcome to Gas Town
claim: Proposes durable work identities and orchestration for many concurrent coding agents.
limit: A strongly opinionated account of a changing tool; advertised throughput tolerates rework and is not independently established here.
use: Study coordination persistence while scrutinizing the cost of tolerated duplication.

author: Robin Hunicke, Marc LeBlanc and Robert Zubek
title: MDA: A Formal Approach to Game Design and Game Research
claim: Connects implemented mechanics, behavior arising during play and the experience sought by players.
limit: A design framework, not an empirical guarantee that a particular mechanic is fun.
use: Work backward from the experience to the rules and their observable consequences.

author: Daniel Cook
title: Loops and Arcs
claim: Explains play through mental models, action, feedback and learning, alongside one-pass experiences.
limit: An influential design essay, not a universal taxonomy or a measure of enjoyment.
use: Ask what the player can learn from an action and try differently afterward.

author: Jeff Orkin
title: Three States and a Plan: The A.I. of F.E.A.R.
claim: Shows how goal-oriented planning and a small action-state interface combine to produce tactical behavior.
limit: A specific shipped game's architecture; it is not an LLM design and planning does not author every expressive detail.
use: Combine authoritative action execution with replaceable choice mechanisms.

author: Michael Mateas and Andrew Stern
title: Structuring Content in the Façade Interactive Drama Architecture
claim: Connects reactive behaviors, drama management and authored story material.
limit: A purpose-built interactive drama with extensive authored structure, not free generation.
use: The interesting narrative problem is often selecting and performing consequences.

author: Emily Short
title: What Does Your Narrative System Need to Do?
claim: Separates narrative functions such as selecting content, offering choices, resolving actions and performing consequences.
limit: Practitioner analysis spanning different narrative forms; requirements depend on the intended experience.
use: Give generated text a defined role in a larger playable system.

author: Georgios N. Yannakakis and Julian Togelius
title: Experience-Driven Procedural Content Generation
claim: Connects generated content, player experience models and evaluation in an optimization process.
limit: Player experience is inferred through imperfect observations and models, not supplied by a universal enjoyment score.
use: Treat objective design and validation as part of generation research.

author: Glenn Fiedler
title: Fix Your Timestep!
claim: Fixed simulation steps, accumulated time and presentation interpolation separate state evolution from display cadence; catch-up work requires headroom.
limit: Numerical-simulation explanation. A fixed step alone does not certify determinism, artistic quality or frame performance.
use: Identify what must advance and what presentation work may be reused.

author: Loopforge studio and independent reviewer
title: Second studio retrospective
claim: Nine interviews, Producer reflection, a separate independent assessment and scoped statistics preserve different accounts of the same work.
limit: Retrospective testimony is not a blind causal experiment; later correction and closure are additive.
use: Reconstruct decisions from attributed accounts and artifacts.

author: Root / Codex
title: I asked a visual studio to work without its eyes
claim: Root documents commissioning an inadequate browser bridge and later host-capability failures.
limit: Agent testimony is an accountable account, not human autobiography or independent corroboration.
use: Put the commissioning agent's choices under the same scrutiny as its delegates.

author: Loopforge studio
title: Checking motion in the running game
claim: Published before/current Forge footage documents a visible correction in the running application.
limit: Viewport and entry context differ; this is not a matched performance experiment, and Sam's later rescue solver was not delivered.
use: Use original-speed motion to judge what numerical pose checks cannot establish.

author: Loopforge Producer
title: What I mistook for progress
claim: The Producer examines how producing artifacts and resolving narrow checks displaced early review of the complete experience.
limit: An attributed retrospective, not proof of hidden motives or the only valid reading of the cycle.
use: Follow one artifact from local correctness to its intended use.

author: Independent systems reviewer
title: A studio needs a shorter path
claim: An independent reading separates useful production work from a workflow that delayed consequential feedback.
limit: Independent authorship does not make this a controlled experiment or direct playtest.
use: Preserve dissent alongside the Producer's account.

author: Loopforge studio; owner merge
title: Day 1 delivery and retained performance result
claim: The combined release reached an ordinary Day 1 ending while retaining the failed final performance comparison and known omissions.
limit: Shipping and subsequent owner merge do not turn the failed benchmark into a pass. The result is specific to its recorded workload and device.
use: Keep the release decision, observed behavior and performance evidence separately inspectable.

author: Loopforge implementation
title: Delivered encounter kernel and contract
claim: A deterministic 50 ms kernel admits actions, reserves resources, applies effects and projects the visible world; planners propose rather than commit.
limit: The authored Day 1 does not implement unrestricted character reasoning, a general BDI system or later-day economic play.
use: Reconstruct a bounded executable model while tracing its relationship to the shipped implementation.

author: Loopforge design and implementation
title: Day 2 implementation boundary
claim: Separates the implemented Day 1 from future staffing, economy, handover and planning systems.
limit: A proposal or defined seam is not implemented capacity.
use: Define the teaching reconstruction without quietly claiming future systems have shipped.

author: Loopforge Engine Master
title: First-cycle interview: preparing a packet and executing it
claim: Engine accepts packet and coverage defects and distinguishes actual host execution from source or fixture evidence.
limit: The testimony explains observed handoff failures; it does not compare alternative staffing arrangements.
use: Keep implementation defects and coordination decisions visible in the same account.

author: Jason Mitchell, Moby Francke and Dhabih Eng
title: Illustrative Rendering in Team Fortress 2
claim: Character silhouettes, restrained detail and shading were designed together to support recognition in play.
limit: A specific art and rendering approach; not a controlled claim that these choices improve every game.
use: Connect visual design to a player’s task; distinguish asset recognition from integrated framing.

author: Don Norman
title: Signifiers, not affordances
claim: Perceivable cues, deliberate or incidental, help people interpret possible actions and social situations.
limit: A conceptual design argument, not an eye-tracking or game comprehension benchmark.
use: Distinguish a usable control from the evidence that lets a player discover and interpret it.

author: Loopforge Visual Artist
title: Second studio interview: composition, dialogue and continuity
claim: Sampled integrated frames exposed occlusion and unstable picture height; the artist revised the preference for anchored balloons.
limit: The artist inspected stills and labelled frame sequences, not uninterrupted playback; does not certify all motion or causal delay.
use: Keep a revised specialist judgment and its concrete tradeoff in the account.

author: Loopforge Scene Director
title: Second studio interview: geography and the receiving exchange
claim: A broad geography view did not reliably show interpersonal exchanges, while changing interface height undermined camera proposals.
limit: Sampled footage and event records support distinct claims; neither certifies full emotional performance.
use: Explain why a shot must serve a particular action, person and recipient.

author: Loopforge Level Designer
title: Second studio interview: routes, control pads and picture bounds
claim: Source geometry and root clearance did not establish visibility of the whole worker at tutorial controls.
limit: Root-disc clearance is narrower than body clearance; still inspection is narrower than continuous motion review.
use: Preserve the useful aisle and room layout while locating a screen-space defect.

author: Loopforge studio
title: Retained first-cycle overlay comparison
claim: The retained before/after captures show a speech balloon moved away from LIMEN’s head at 14.65 seconds.
limit: A scoped overlay correction, not a complete animation, grounding or live-layout pass.
use: Show an actual repair before testing its limits across a changing scene.

author: Charles Packer and colleagues
title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
claim: Explicit movement between external stores and active context supports extended conversation and document tasks.
limit: Storage capacity and reliable use of a particular record are separate questions.
use: Follow a saved fact all the way into the input that can change a decision.

author: Nelson F. Liu and colleagues
title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
claim: Position of relevant information changes performance on the studied multi-document QA and key-value retrieval tasks.
limit: Historical models and task designs; no universal contemporary performance curve is claimed.
use: Distinguish accepting a long input from effectively using its contents.

author: Loopforge published production history
title: A private build and a story beyond day one: the memory installation
claim: Native memory discovery and indexing were observed; source-attributed retrieval in existing sessions was not established. Recall was later saved Off; craft files and foundation receipts remained usable.
limit: This record does not measure the counterfactual effect of retrieval on delivered work.
use: Separate infrastructure presence from a record actually informing a decision.

author: Loopforge Engine Master
title: Second studio interview: custody, hearing and the action boundary
claim: The export retains Ed’s custody without giving Bob the same knowledge; hearing rules expose missed staging.
limit: The local typed runtime is not a general BDI planner or proof of complete legacy transport compatibility.
use: Identify a useful shipped separation without inflating the architecture.

author: Anand S. Rao and Michael P. Georgeff
title: BDI Agents: From Theory to Practice
claim: Separates informational, motivational and deliberative states under limited sensing and changing environments.
limit: The theory and practical interpreter are larger commitments than a dictionary of character beliefs.
use: Why a model’s information need not equal the environment’s state.

author: Loopforge studio
title: Pinned encounter kernel: reported claims and observed transfers
claim: Received claims write reported beliefs; selected observers receive transfer facts. The player projection excludes private belief records.
limit: Explicit rules and observer lists, not a general perception or credibility model.
use: Keep testimony, observation and world mutation separate.

author: Loopforge Writer
title: Second studio interview: listeners, choices and handoffs
claim: Withdraws blanket audience edits after distinguishing twelve staging repairs from four valid nonreceipts. Q5 describes replacing an automatic Theatre benefit with requests and a practice-versus-output choice in a later proposal.
limit: Sampled frames and hearing events do not certify continuous performance. The cohort correction is authored source, not delivered Day 1 gameplay or a player study.
use: Distinguish legitimate missing knowledge from a broken exchange; connect later narrative choices to requests and consequences.

author: Loopforge studio
title: Pinned Day 1 hearing-staging regression
claim: Runs the sequence to assert twelve selected repaired receipts, four genuine nonreceipts and durable closing consequences.
limit: State and receipt assertions do not establish the emotional quality of animation or dialogue.
use: Test required delivery while preserving intentional ignorance.

author: Loopforge studio
title: Pinned arrival layout and spatial hearing rule
claim: Local and shouted channels use 6/18-metre ranges; cross-room hearing also requires an audible portal and a line through the arrival doorway.
limit: A deliberately compact spatial rule, not an acoustic simulation.
use: Let placement repair a missed exchange without silently broadening perception.

author: Nels Anderson, interviewed by Dillon Wilson
title: Interview: Nels Anderson on Mark of the Ninja
claim: Visible noise reach and awareness cues help players reason about stealth encounters.
limit: Design testimony from one game, not a controlled test or a demand to reveal all hidden state.
use: Distinguish understandable perception rules from omniscient characters.

author: Loopforge Critic
title: Second studio interview: the limits of sampled views
claim: Actual stills and ordered frames revealed obstructed views, misleading labels and an arms-out departure pose.
limit: The Critic did not claim continuous video or live play; the packet cannot establish motion quality between samples.
use: Locate a presentation finding in the actual evidence inspected.

author: Independent systems reviewer
title: An autonomous studio needs a usable feedback loop
claim: Producer recovered native browser operation, while the wider craft review loop remained only partly established.
limit: The assessment shares selected evidence and commission framing; independent authorship is not blinding or causal identification.
use: Test Root’s explanation against access requirements and errors already addressable without a browser.

author: Bret Victor
title: Learnable Programming
claim: A programming environment should make execution and state inspectable, including their relationships over time.
limit: A design argument for human understanding, not an empirical result about language-model agents.
use: Distinguish immediate final output from an inspectable process.

author: Loopforge studio · Animator
title: Animator — second studio interview
claim: Documents sampled pose judgments, rig and wrapper failures, release-before-rise ordering and the bounded rejection of Sam’s waist path.
limit: Selected decoded frames, not continuous playback. Tentative actor attribution, contact continuity and precision performance remain unresolved.
use: Compare action meaning and shared contacts with a named state or technically valid bank.

author: John Lasseter
title: Principles of Traditional Animation Applied to 3D Computer Animation
claim: Timing, anticipation and follow-through contribute to readable action beyond interpolating poses.
limit: Practice-based argument with animated examples, not a controlled result on game workers or agent animation.
use: Frame preparation and recovery as authored choices. Primary paper pp. 37–39 inspected; no figures republished.

author: David Rosen · Wolfire Games
title: An Indie Approach to Procedural Animation
claim: Combines responsive movement, procedural refinements and performance-focused keyframes.
limit: Slide deck inspected; embedded motion demonstrations and the full spoken talk were not reviewed here. It does not validate Loopforge’s approach.
use: A hybrid production method, qualified by the studio’s failed and improved contact work.

author: Bernardino Romera-Paredes and colleagues
title: Mathematical discoveries from program search with large language models
claim: Generated programs enter an executable evaluation and selection loop, with successful programs informing subsequent proposals.
limit: Cap-set and bin-packing settings offer usable evaluators; this does not validate subjective creative judgments.
use: Separate an executable proposal from a convincing account of its success. Figure 1 reproduced under CC BY 4.0.

author: Andrej Karpathy
title: autoresearch — README and experiment instructions
claim: Bounds editable training code, training time and a fixed validation metric while retaining experiment outcomes.
limit: Hardware and budget affect comparability. A project method, not a controlled claim about autonomous research productivity.
use: Candidate improvements and changes to their evaluator need separate, visible decisions. program.md blob dea9bcc0174f1502d0ba64000b94b81ba605855b inspected.

author: Emily Short
title: Storylets: You Want Them
claim: Defines a storylet through content, prerequisites and effects, while leaving size and selection open.
limit: A design vocabulary and examples, not a controlled study of player response.
use: Specify when a passage belongs and what it changes.

author: Failbetter Games
title: StoryNexus Developer Diary #2: fewer spreadsheets, less swearing
claim: Agreed quality-change rules support collaborative additions; short setup-choice-result cycles can hinder long scenes.
limit: Historical product rationale, not current platform guidance or a claim that modularity removes authoring costs.
use: Make effects legible to collaborators without mistaking unit size for dramatic rhythm.

author: Michael Mateas and Andrew Stern
title: Writing Façade: A Case Study in Procedural Authorship
claim: The drinks example combines dialogue, interruptions, re-establishment and staging; the authors report costly content work and limited global agency.
limit: A retrospective of a specific interactive drama; no current generative-model performance claim. Page article date is February 2008; unrelated May 2004 text belongs to neighboring content.
use: Commission resumable dramatic actions rather than isolated fluent lines.

author: Bruno Dias
title: Attempted: Building a general-purpose QBN system
claim: Distinguishes narrative, text and UI engines; describes scope and authoring-tool compromises that stopped a general-purpose system.
limit: One builder’s experience, not evidence that reusable narrative systems cannot work. Historical tool-status claims are not repeated as current facts.
use: Prove a small authoring workflow before generalizing its format.

author: Edsger W. Dijkstra
title: Notes on Structured Programming — EWD249
claim: Correctness reasoning relies on stated properties of the implementation; the equality example shows an apparently helpful deviation breaking an assumed property.
limit: Read in the University of Texas archive transcription, especially “On the validity of proofs versus the validity of implementations.” This is not an evaluation of contemporary agents.
use: Make assumptions at implementation boundaries explicit.

author: Koen Claessen and John Hughes
title: QuickCheck: A lightweight tool for random testing of Haskell programs
claim: Properties expressed as Haskell functions can be tested with random inputs and custom generators.
limit: The primary university publication record and abstract were inspected, not the full paper. No detailed case-study or shrinking claim is attributed to it here.
use: Separate the property being asserted from the examples used to exercise it.

author: Hamel Husain
title: Your AI Product Needs Evals
claim: Task-specific assertions and contextual trace review serve different parts of evaluation and debugging.
limit: A practitioner account centered on Lucy/Rechat; not a controlled causal study of every proposed practice.
use: Design the inspection surface around the evidence required by the judgment.

author: Hamel Husain
title: Using LLM-as-a-Judge For Evaluation: A Complete Guide
claim: Raw agreement can hide failure on a rare label; prompt, development and final test examples serve distinct roles.
limit: The revised guide was inspected on 26 October 2026. This chapter’s twenty records are authored arithmetic, not a model-evaluation experiment.
use: Examine both kinds of error before trusting a judge.

author: Casey Muratori
title: Walk Monster
claim: An exploration strategy densely covered an exterior while neglecting a room; changing target selection improved its fit to reachability inspection.
limit: A specific movement-tool account for The Witness. No universal algorithm ranking or current product claim.
use: Inspect the distribution of attempts, not just their quantity.

author: Camilo Gordillo, Joakim Bergdahl, Konrad Tollmar and Linus Gisslén
title: Improving Playtesting Coverage via Curiosity Driven Reinforcement Learning Agents
claim: Count-based spatial novelty and resets at previously reached grounded positions support navigation exploration.
limit: The authored three-dimensional navigation study does not measure narrative-state coverage or player enjoyment.
use: Define the state distinctions a coverage measure preserves.

author: Loopforge Engine Master
title: Second studio interview, Q3: assignment and physical occupancy
claim: Level’s paired-work counterexample exposed a display counting assignment rather than both physical occupants.
limit: A reported correction, not a measured incidence or controlled comparison of exploration methods.
use: Add meaningful occupancy conditions to a place-based test plan.

author: Jonas Gillberg, Joakim Bergdahl, Alessandro Sestini, Andrew Eakins and Linus Gisslén
title: Technical Challenges of Deploying Reinforcement Learning Agents for Game Testing in AAA Games
claim: Learned locomotion complemented scripted testing; accelerated simulation exposed physics failures.
limit: Specific production integrations in Battlefield 2042 and Dead Space, not evidence that automation removes human playtesting.
use: Preserve the meaning of the environment while increasing sample throughput.

author: Alex Zook, Josef Spjut and Jonathan Tremblay
title: Fly, Fail, Fix: Iterative Game Repair with Reinforcement Learning and Large Multimodal Models
claim: A fixed automated player supplied useful feedback for configuration repair; preliminary physics changes exposed player brittleness.
limit: The target was a score in Flappy Bird. The two scripted birds here are a separate authored study, not replication or human evidence.
use: Keep the tested player population visible in an optimization claim.

author: Mike Ambinder
title: Valve’s Approach to Playtesting: The Application of Empiricism
claim: Observation, verbal reports and aggregate measures answer different questions and introduce different biases.
limit: Slides inspected, including direct-observation and method tradeoffs; no talk video or physiological claims used.
use: Choose an observation around a design question before explaining the intended solution.

author: Loopforge implementation and retained test record
title: Matched opening optimization: result and provenance
claim: The same opening scene and assets passed after a bundle of local reuse and deferral changes; long pauses fell from 31 to 4.
limit: One matched before/after run on Intel HD 620. Individual changes were not isolated; phones, cold loading and later scenes are not certified.
use: Compare a recurring-work reduction with its unchanged visible commission.

author: Loopforge retained performance export
title: Opening revision 12: ten-minute run and long-frame events
claim: Twenty-eight frames exceeded 100 ms; fifteen occurred in the passage shot. The export retains elapsed time, duration, shot and phase for each.
limit: A specific working-machine run. Event location is not CPU/GPU causal attribution; only long events, not all frames, are retained as timestamps.
use: Aim a profile at the observed workload without inventing a continuous trace.

author: Loopforge implementation and performance record
title: Graphics comparison and repeated reference
claim: The reference repeat drifted from 23.6 to 20.5 FPS, limiting causal interpretation of individual settings.
limit: An earlier 26-actor fixture with different workload and protocol from opening or Day 1 acceptance. Not a precise setting speedup.
use: Spend on a meaningful comparison before committing an optimization task.

author: Fabian Giesen
title: Optimizing Software Occlusion Culling: The Reckoning
claim: Several high-return repairs affected surrounding framework code; unexpectedly costly operations can be better targets than expected hotspots.
limit: A specific native graphics implementation, not a benchmark of contemporary browser rendering or AI coding.
use: Judge a proposed optimization by its useful gain and disruption.

author: Paul Lewis
title: Rendering performance
claim: Rendering changes trigger different portions of the pixel pipeline, and animation cadence differs from discrete interaction response.
limit: Browser-pipeline guidance, not attribution of Loopforge WebGL stalls or a field-speed measurement.
use: Commission a visual result with an explicit recurring-work budget.

author: Loopforge production record
title: Combined Day 1 review candidate
claim: Records selected Max control work, retained delivered Sam motion and excluded experimental solver modules.
limit: Written before final release review and owner merge; later delivery evidence is additive.
use: Separate installed work, preserved inquiry and deferred corrections.

author: Loopforge studio
title: Second retrospective: scoped resource ledger
claim: Nonnegative within-session deltas establish an observed lower bound across ten native roles for a fixed interval.
limit: Excludes Root, opening boundaries, unsampled tails, resets and later work; field mapping is inherited and billed money unavailable.
use: Keep resource observations distinct from a full cost account or productivity ratio.

author: Nicole Forsgren
title: Navigating the SPACE between productivity and developer happiness
claim: Activity and volume miss important contributions to software outcomes; SPACE considers several dimensions of developer productivity.
limit: An author’s account of human software development, not a measure of agent experience or an agent benchmark.
use: Ask what a machine-activity ledger leaves unmeasured.

author: Loopforge design record
title: Day Two boundary
claim: Preserves future-day boundaries separately from the delivered first-day encounter.
limit: A design boundary does not establish an implemented second day or general planner.
use: Commission a small consequential experiment before a larger continuation.

author: Stripe
title: Idempotent requests — API v1 contract
claim: An operation key lets API v1 callers recover the saved response after execution begins. Validation, conflicts and key retention have explicit boundaries.
limit: A specific API contract, not proof of global exactly-once execution. API v2 behavior differs; the chapter discusses v1.
use: What must an agent know before retrying an uncertain side effect?

author: Jeffrey Dean and Luiz André Barroso
title: The Tail at Scale
claim: Occasional slow components can dominate the response time of a large interactive service.
limit: Large-service engineering evidence; the six-investigation timeline in this book is an authored illustration, not a measurement from the paper or of AI agents.
use: Which required branch determines when the recipient can continue?

author: Root / Codex
title: Close-cycle audit: repairs, feedback and scoped usage
claim: A later 7h50 correction window records repaired samples, validation work, delayed visual rejection and native-studio usage.
limit: Frozen at 23:50 UTC; no matching corrected after-video then. Root, independent review, later tails and billed cost excluded.
use: Distinguish useful repairs, reusable machinery and unfinished creative payoff.

author: Loopforge studio; Root / Codex
title: Additive outcome and closure record
claim: Later footage and reviewed selection were delivered; the owner stopped further corrections with performance failures retained.
limit: Native closure preceded the owner’s 26 October 18:01 UTC merge. Sampled review is not full physical or performance acceptance.
use: Keep the stopping decision and Root’s coordination errors inside the system boundary.

author: Fantine Huot and colleagues
title: Agents’ Room: Narrative Generation through Multi-step Collaboration
claim: Specialized sequential planning and writing improved expert preference over evaluated story-generation baselines.
limit: Same backbone does not establish equal total cost; output lengths differ. Not a parallel swarm-speed experiment.
use: Can specialization improve judged story quality without shortening elapsed work?

author: Hyunseung Lim and colleagues
title: Understanding Human–Multi-Agent Team Formation for Creative Work
claim: Twelve design practitioners revised AI-team arrangements toward direct human orchestration.
limit: A technology-probe ideation study, not a causal production-efficiency estimate for every creative team.
use: Where must a value judgment remain available to change the direction?

author: Anil R. Doshi and Oliver P. Hauser
title: Generative AI enhances individual creativity but reduces the collective diversity of novel content
claim: Generated ideas improved evaluated short stories while their collective outputs became more similar.
limit: Human writing with AI starting ideas, not an autonomous-team or game-production trial.
use: Does a larger batch improve individual candidates while narrowing useful choice?

author: Yun Wan and Yoram M. Kalman
title: Using Generative AI Personas Increases Collective Diversity in Human Ideation
claim: A modified story-writing study used deliberately different personas to generate more varied starting plots.
limit: Persona-conditioned generation and human writing; no proof of independent agent reasoning or production speed.
use: Test diversity in the retained outputs, not the number of named roles.

author: Wilson Lin
title: Scaling long-running autonomous coding
claim: Changing coordination and removing a bottlenecking integrator supported larger autonomous coding runs.
limit: Vendor experiments with differing completion states; not controlled evidence of equal-budget creative efficiency.
use: Does another coordination role shorten the path to accepted work?
